transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's... it's just been really hard lately. I mean, my daughter, she just left for basic training, and I knew it was coming, you know? We talked about it for months, got all her gear sorted, went to the recruiter's office together. But since she actually packed up and left... I just feel like I come home to a completely dead house. It's so quiet it rings in my ears. And I just can't seem to keep myself together at all. I've been sitting in my truck before my shifts at the shop—I'm a sheet metal worker, have been for years—and I just sit there in the cab, crying my eyes out before I even clock in. 

And then when I'm on the floor, I'm messing up. I'm missing steps on welding jobs that I could do in my sleep, jobs I've done a thousand times. It's embarrassing, honestly. And I'm snapping at the younger guys in the shop, which isn't fair to them, but I just have zero patience right now. I don't even know who I am at this point. I usually love getting out on the water on my days off, or working on this metal sculpture I've been building in the garage, but I haven't touched any of it. I just... I look at it all and I just don't see the point anymore. I just feel completely stuck since she left.
How long have you been feeling this way since your daughter left for basic training?

Well, let's see... she shipped out exactly a month ago. Yeah, it's been about a month now. I remember because it was a Tuesday, pouring rain, which just felt so heavy, you know? Like the sky was matching my mood. We drove down to the processing station, and she had this huge green duffel bag, and she just looked so young walking through those double doors. 

And honestly, from that exact moment, from that Tuesday a month ago, it's just been this massive struggle. I drove back to the house, and I walked in, and the silence just hit me like a physical blow. So, yeah, for this whole past month, every single day has been like... like wading through wet cement. I kept telling myself, you know, maybe week two will be better, maybe by week three I'll get my head on straight and get back to normal at the shop. But here we are, a whole month down the line, and I’m still sitting in the cab of my truck crying before my shift. It hasn't let up at all. Not for a single day in the last four weeks. I just can't seem to shake it.
Are you still getting any pleasure from things you used to enjoy?

No, not really. I mean, I tried. Last weekend, the weather was actually decent for once, not too hot, and I thought, okay, I'm going to take the boat out. I usually love being out on the water, you know? Just the smell of the lake, the sound of the water against the hull... it usually clears my head. I used to go out every Sunday morning, sometimes my daughter would come with me, sometimes it was just me. So I hitched it up, drove all the way to the marina, paid the launch fee, and I got it in the water. But I just sat there. I didn't even turn the key. I looked out at the lake and it just looked... flat. Gray. Like all the color was sucked out of it. I ended up pulling the boat right back out after maybe twenty minutes. 

And my sculpture in the garage... I've been working on this big heron made out of scrap steel and copper wire for, gosh, six months now. I was so excited about getting the wings just right, getting the patina on the copper to look like feathers. I have all my tools set out, my torch is right there, but I walk into the garage and I just look at it and feel absolutely nothing. It’s just pieces of metal now. It doesn't excite me. It feels like a chore even thinking about putting on my safety glasses. I used to spend hours out there, lose track of time, forget to eat dinner because I was so focused. Now, I just turn the light off and go back inside to sit on the couch. So, yeah, everything I used to love just feels completely empty right now.
Do you feel guilty about your daughter leaving for basic training?

No, it's not guilt, exactly. I mean, I don't feel like I did something wrong by letting her go or anything like that. We talked about it so much, you know? Since she was in her junior year of high school, she kept bringing home those pamphlets with the crisp uniforms and the flags, and we'd sit at the kitchen table for hours going over the pros and cons. The GI Bill, the discipline, the travel... I supported her 100 percent. I even helped her train for the physical fitness test—we'd go running at the high school track every Saturday morning at 6 AM, rain or shine. I was the one holding the stopwatch while she did push-ups in the driveway. 

So, I don't feel guilty that she's there. I know it's what she wants, and I know she's strong enough to handle it. She's a tough kid. She gets that from me, I think, working in the shop all these years, you have to have a thick skin. But it's not guilt. It's more just... this overwhelming absence. Like a piece of the foundation of my house just vanished overnight, and now everything is leaning and creaking and I don't know how to prop it back up. I don't feel bad that she left, I just... I just don't know how to be here without her. It's just me and this big, empty house, and all the routines we had, the Saturday morning runs, the dinners where we'd complain about our days... it's all just gone. So no, not guilty. Just lost, I guess. Really, really lost.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could join your daughter wherever she is?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know I'm struggling, I know I'm crying in the truck and I can't look at my sculptures, but I don't want to die. I'm not sitting here thinking about ending it all. I know she's going to come back, you know? Eventually, she'll graduate basic, she'll get her assignment, and I'll get to see her again. I just have to figure out how to get through this part, this middle part where everything is just so quiet. 

And as for wishing I could join her... well, I mean, part of me wishes I could just be a fly on the wall, just to see her in her uniform, to see her doing the obstacle courses and yelling the cadences. We used to watch those documentaries on the military channel, the ones about boot camp, and she'd point at the screen and say, "That's going to be me, Mom." So yeah, I wish I could see that. I wish I could be there to cheer her on, or maybe just to make sure she's eating enough, because she always used to skip breakfast before school and I'd have to hand her a granola bar as she was running out the door. But I don't literally want to join her. I'm thirty-eight, I've got a bad shoulder from working sheet metal for fifteen years, I couldn't do those push-ups anymore even if I tried. And I know she needs to do this on her own. This is her journey, her career. It's just... it's just hard being the one left behind in the quiet house, you know? But no, I don't want to not be here. I just want it to stop hurting so much while I'm waiting for her to call.
Have you been avoiding social interactions or spending time with friends and family since your daughter left?

Well, I don't know if I'd say I'm avoiding people on purpose, like, hiding in the house with the curtains drawn or anything. But I haven't really been going out, either. My sister, Sarah, she lives about forty minutes away in the next county over, and she usually hosts this big barbecue on the last Sunday of the month. She has this huge backyard with a pool, and all the cousins come over, and it's usually this loud, chaotic thing. I've gone every month for the last three years. But this last time, a couple of weeks ago, I just... I couldn't do it. She called me on Thursday to see what I was bringing—I usually make this potato salad that everyone loves, the one with the dill and the hard-boiled eggs—and I just told her I wasn't feeling up to it. I think I blamed it on a headache, or maybe I said my shoulder was acting up again from work. I can't even remember the exact excuse.

And it's not just family. The guys at the shop, we usually go grab a beer at O'Malley's after our shift on Fridays. It's kind of a tradition. We wash up, change out of our work boots, and just go complain about the foreman for an hour or two before heading home. I haven't been in... gosh, since before she left. Last Friday, Dave—he's the guy who works the plasma cutter next to my station—he actually came over and tapped me on the shoulder and said, "Hey, you coming with us today? First round's on me." And I just looked at him and said no, I had to get home. 

It's just that, if I go, people are going to ask. They're going to say, "How's she doing?" or "Have you heard from her?" or "Wow, the house must be so quiet!" And they mean well, I know they do. Dave's got two kids in college, he gets the empty nest thing, sort of. But I just don't have the energy to put on that fake smile and say, "Oh, she's doing great, I'm so proud of her," while inside I feel like I'm drowning. I don't want to sit at a bar or a backyard barbecue and try to make small talk about the weather or the football game when all I can think about is whether she's okay, whether she's sleeping, whether she misses me as much as I miss her. It just takes too much effort to pretend I'm normal right now. So I just go home, park the truck, and go inside. It's easier that way, you know? Just... easier to be alone, even if it's miserable.
Are there any activities that you still find yourself looking forward to or enjoying, even if it's just a little bit?

I mean, I try to think of things. I really do. But... no, not really. I used to have things, you know? Like, I used to really look forward to Sunday mornings. Before she left, Sunday was always our lazy day. I’d get up early and make pancakes—blueberry, usually, because she loved them, even though I almost always burned the first batch because the big cast-iron skillet I use heats up totally unevenly on the left side of my stove. 

And then, after breakfast, I’d go out to the garage. I have this old '98 Chevy Silverado. It’s got a lot of rust on the quarter panels, but I’ve always loved tinkering with it. I’d roll the garage door up, put on the classic rock station—104.5, they do this "no repeat weekend" thing—and I'd just spend hours out there. I'd be replacing spark plugs or messing with the brake pads, getting grease all under my fingernails, while my daughter was inside doing her homework or watching those true crime shows she’s so obsessed with. It was just... peaceful, you know? I’d look forward to that garage time all week when I was stuck at the shop doing the exact same cuts on the sheet metal over and over and over again. It was my time to just zone out.

But now... I don't know. I went out to the garage last Sunday. I thought to myself, okay, I'm going to change the oil. I need to do something. I bought the filter at AutoZone on Friday after work, I had the drain pan ready, I had the cardboard laid out to slide under the chassis. I opened the garage door, turned on the radio, and I just... I stood there holding the socket wrench for maybe twenty minutes. I didn't even get under the truck. The song on the radio changed three times, I think it went from Aerosmith to Tom Petty, and I just felt so heavy. I didn't care about the oil. I didn't care about the truck at all. The music just sounded like noise, this grating, awful noise echoing off the concrete. 

I ended up just turning the radio off, putting the wrench down on the workbench, and going back inside to sit on the couch. I didn't even turn the TV on. I just sat there looking at the wall. So, no, I can't really say I look forward to anything right now. It's like... everything I used to like doing just reminds me that she's not here, or it just feels completely pointless. Even the stuff that had nothing to do with her, like the truck. It just feels like going through the motions, and I don't have the energy to fake it, even for myself. I just don't care about the truck, or the pancakes, or any of it.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy or look forward to, even if it's just a little?

Like I... like I was just saying with the truck and the garage, no. There really isn't anything. I know it probably sounds like I'm just being stubborn or, I don't know, not trying hard enough to snap out of it, but I promise you, I've racked my brain trying to find just one little thing to look forward to. 

I mean, my coworker Brenda—she works in the office at the shop, doing the payroll and all the invoices—she kept telling me I should try reading. She's always bringing these thick thriller novels into the breakroom, the ones with the raised foil letters on the covers. She said they're great for taking your mind off things because they have all these crazy plot twists and you get sucked right in. So I actually listened to her. I went to the Goodwill down on 4th Street last Tuesday on my lunch break and bought three of them for like fifty cents each. I figured, why not? It's cheap, it's quiet. 

I brought them home, sat down in my recliner, opened the first one... and I swear to you, I read the same paragraph on the very first page maybe ten or twelve times. I couldn't tell you a single character's name or what the book was even about. It was just words on paper. My eyes were moving across the page, but my brain was just... somewhere else. Probably wondering what they were serving my daughter in the mess hall, or if her boots were giving her blisters, because she always had such sensitive heels when she played soccer in middle school. 

I ended up just putting the book down on the coffee table next to this stack of junk mail I haven't even bothered to open since she left. So, no, whether it's fixing my truck, or making breakfast, or trying to read a cheap paperback... there's just zero enjoyment. It's like someone just went to the breaker box in my head and flipped all the switches to off. I just don't have a single thing that makes me feel good right now.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight since your daughter left for basic training?

I... I really couldn't tell you. I haven't stepped on a scale in I don't know how long. I have this old dial scale in the bathroom, not one of those fancy digital ones that tells you your body fat or whatever, just a cheap white plastic thing I got at Walmart or maybe Target a few years back. It’s shoved way back under the bathroom sink, behind a giant family-sized bottle of mouthwash and some extra toilet paper rolls. I haven't even pulled it out to look at it since before she left. Why would I, you know? It's just... it's not something I care about right now. 

And as for how my clothes fit, it's hard to gauge. I wear the same heavy denim jeans and thick, long-sleeved cotton shirts to the shop every single day. You have to wear thick, durable stuff when you're working with sheet metal, otherwise you're coming home with cuts and scrapes all over your arms and legs from the sharp edges off the cutter. My work clothes are always kind of baggy anyway so I can move around and bend over the table, and I always wear this thick leather belt I got at Tractor Supply to keep everything up. I guess I might be pulling the belt a notch tighter lately? Or maybe my jeans are just stretched out because I haven't been doing laundry as much. I used to do laundry every Sunday without fail, separating all her clothes from my greasy work stuff, but now I just kind of throw whatever I need into the wash whenever I completely run out of clean socks. 

So, honestly, I have absolutely no idea if I've gained or lost anything. I just haven't been paying any attention to my body or how I look. I haven't even really looked in the mirror properly, aside from just tying my hair back before my shift. I'm just surviving day to day, so my weight hasn't even crossed my mind.
Have you been having trouble sleeping since your daughter left for basic training?

I mean... no, not really. Sleep is probably the one thing that hasn't changed. If anything, I just pass right out. I work ten-hour shifts on my feet on solid concrete, hauling around heavy-gauge aluminum and steel sheets all day, so by the time I get home, my body is just completely shot. I usually take a hot shower just to get the metal dust and the grease off my arms and out of my hair, and then I just crash. 

I have this older queen-sized mattress—it’s not great, the springs kind of squeak on the left side if you move too fast, but I bought this thick memory foam topper for it at Kohl's a couple of years ago when they were doing one of those big holiday weekend clearance sales. Best sixty bucks I ever spent, honestly, because it really helps with my lower back after bending over the cutting tables all day. Anyway, I usually just crawl into bed around 8:30 or 9:00, and I'm out the second my head hits the pillow. 

I have this old digital alarm clock on my nightstand, the kind with the really bright, annoying red numbers that sort of glow in the dark and cast this weird red light on the ceiling. I just stare at that for maybe two minutes, and then I'm just gone. I don't wake up tossing and turning, I don't wake up in the middle of the night needing a glass of water, nothing like that. I just sleep straight through like a rock until that awful buzzer goes off at 4:30 in the morning. It's almost like my brain just wants to shut off so I don't have to sit there awake in the quiet house, you know? Since it's just me now, the house gets so loud with all the little creaks and the hum of the refrigerator, and I just don't want to hear it. So, yeah, no trouble sleeping at all. I just close my eyes and I'm dead to the world until I have to get up and do it all over again.
Do you feel sad most of the day, every day, since your daughter left for basic training?

I wouldn't say I feel *sad*... not like crying all day or anything like that. It's not that kind of feeling. I mean, when she first left, I did cry. We were standing by the Greyhound bus down at the station on Elm—the one with the flickering neon sign that never seems to get fixed—and she had her duffel bag slung over her shoulder. She looked so small, you know? Even though she's eighteen, she just looked like my little girl. I cried then, and I cried on the drive home, gripping the steering wheel so hard my knuckles were white. 

But since then? It's not sadness, exactly. It's more like... emptiness. Like the house is just a hollow shell and I'm just rattling around inside it. I go to work, I cut the sheet metal, I talk to Brenda in the breakroom about her thrillers or whatever, I come home, I shower, I sleep. It's just a routine. I don't feel like sitting on the couch weeping. I just feel heavy, I guess. Like there's a wet wool blanket draped over my shoulders all the time. 

And it's weird because people expect you to be sad. My sister called me last week from Ohio—she lives out there with her husband who manages a string of car washes—and she kept using that soft, pitying voice people use at funerals. Asking me how I was holding up, telling me it's okay to cry. But I didn't want to cry. I just wanted to get off the phone so I could go back to staring at the wall in the living room. 

It's just this constant, dull ache of her not being here. I walk past her bedroom door, which I keep shut now because I can't stand looking at her perfectly made bed and all her high school track trophies on the shelf. I don't burst into tears when I see the door. I just feel... nothing. Just flat. So, no, I wouldn't call it sad most of the day. Just empty. Like all the color got washed out of everything the minute that bus pulled away from the curb.
Are there any small things that still bring you a bit of pleasure or interest?

I... I really don't think so. I mean, I've tried to think about that, you know? Because people always say you should find little things to keep you going, like a hobby or whatever. Brenda at work—she's the one I eat lunch with, she's been at the shop for like fifteen years and knows everyone's business—she brought in this huge Tupperware container of homemade snickerdoodles the other day. She knows I usually love them. She uses this specific recipe from her grandmother that has a little bit of cream of tartar in it, makes them really soft in the middle but crispy on the edges. And she pushed this big plate of them right in front of me in the breakroom, practically begging me to take one. 

I took a bite, just to be polite, because she went to all that trouble, but it just tasted like... I don't know, cardboard? Sand? I couldn't even finish it. I just wrapped the rest of it in a paper towel and threw it in the trash when she wasn't looking. It's like my taste buds just shut off. 

And it's not just food. I used to really like watching this one home renovation show on HGTV on Thursday nights. The one where they take these awful, run-down houses in Texas and fix them up. My daughter and I used to sit on the couch and make fun of the ugly tile choices or the weird paint colors they'd pick. We'd have a whole running commentary going. But last Thursday, I turned the TV on, found the channel, and just sat there staring at the screen. I didn't care about the shiplap, I didn't care about the open-concept kitchen. I just watched the people moving around on the screen and realized I hadn't actually heard a single word they said for like twenty minutes. 

I even tried going to the hardware store over the weekend, just to walk around. I usually love the smell of the lumber aisle, you know? That fresh-cut pine smell. I was thinking maybe I'd build a little birdhouse or something for the backyard, just to keep my hands busy on a Sunday. But I got to the aisle, stood there looking at all the two-by-fours, and I just felt so incredibly tired. I didn't even buy anything. I just turned around, walked back out to my truck, and drove home. 

So, no. There isn't really anything. It's all just... flat. Everything I used to care about or find interesting just seems completely pointless now. I just go through the motions, but none of it actually means anything to me anymore.
Are there any activities that you've stopped doing since your daughter left that you used to find enjoyable?

I mean, yeah, there are things I used to do, but... I just haven't. Like going out on the water. We have this little aluminum johnboat, nothing fancy at all, just a little fourteen-footer with an old Evinrude outboard motor that I spent like three weekends fixing up last spring. I used to take it out on the lake on Sunday mornings. Sometimes my daughter would come, or sometimes I'd just go by myself to clear my head and watch the sun come up over the tree line. But now? I haven't even taken the blue tarp off it. It's just sitting in the side yard collecting pine needles. 

And my sculptures, too. I used to take scrap metal from the shop—just little off-cuts of aluminum and mild steel that were going to the recycling bin anyway—and I'd bring them home and weld them together in the garage. I'd make these little abstract pieces, birds and dogs, things like that. It was relaxing. But I haven't touched my welding torch at home in weeks. I just look at the metal and I don't see the point anymore. 

It all just comes back to the fact that since she left for basic training, I feel like I come home to a dead house, and I just... I can’t keep myself together. It's like I'm falling apart at the seams, honestly. It's not just at home, either, it's bleeding into everything. Half the time, I'm sitting out in my truck in the shop parking lot before my shifts, just gripping the steering wheel and crying my eyes out. Just sitting there bawling until I have to wipe my face with a fast-food napkin and go inside and pretend I'm fine. 

But I'm not fine. I'm actually messing up at work, which is really bad because I'm usually the one the foreman relies on. I'm missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for literally years—basic TIG welding seams that I could normally do in my sleep, and I'm blowing through the metal or messing up the bead because my brain is just somewhere else. And then I get frustrated, and I end up snapping at the younger guys on the floor. There's this one kid, Tyler, he's just an apprentice, barely older than my daughter, and I completely bit his head off on Tuesday just because he asked to borrow my angle grinder. I felt terrible about it later, but my nerves are just so completely shot. I just don't have the patience or the energy for any of it anymore, let alone hobbies.
Do you feel depressed most of the day?

I don't... I don't know if I'd use that word. Depressed. Because when I hear that word, I think of, you know, those commercials on TV with the lady staring out a rainy window looking miserable, or... well, like my Aunt Carol. She's my mom's older sister, lives up in Dayton, and she had real, actual depression back in the nineties. Like, she wouldn't get out of bed for weeks at a time. We'd go over there to check on her, and the house would be pitch black, all the curtains pulled tight, smelling like stale cigarettes and unwashed laundry, and she wouldn't even get up to feed her own cats. That's what being depressed most of the day looks like to me. 

But me? I get out of bed. I make my coffee—just Folgers, nothing fancy, I use the same old drip machine I've had for ten years—and I pack my lunch, usually just some turkey on wheat and a bag of pretzels, and I lace up my steel-toed boots. I drive to the shop every single day. I'm functioning, mostly. I mean, yeah, I just told you about how I break down in the truck before my shift, and how my nerves are shot and I'm messing up my welds and snapping at poor Tyler, but once I'm actually on the floor? When I've got my welding hood down and the sparks are flying and the shop radio is blasting some classic rock station over the noise of the grinders? I'm not sitting there feeling depressed. 

I'm just... running on empty. Autopilot. It’s exactly like I was saying before about not feeling sad most of the day. It's not this deep, dark depression from morning till night. It's just a big, blank space where my normal life used to be before she got on that Greyhound. The breakdowns in the truck, that's just... that's just the pressure boiling over, I guess. But the rest of the day, the bulk of the day? I'm just going through the motions. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed most of the day. I'm just trying to survive until it's time to clock out.
Do you find that you have less interest in the things you used to enjoy compared to before your daughter left?

Oh, completely. It's... it's like a night and day difference, honestly. Because I was managing just fine before my daughter shipped out. I really was. I mean, we were so busy those last couple of months, running around town getting those specific thick green socks the recruiter told her to buy, making sure all her paperwork was in order, having family over for a going-away dinner... I was stressed, sure, but a normal kind of stressed. I was still doing my metal sculptures in the garage after work, still taking the boat out. 

I actually remember the Sunday right before she left. I was out on the water by 6 AM, drinking my coffee out of this old dented Stanley thermos I take everywhere, just watching the mist burn off the lake. I felt completely normal. I enjoyed it. It felt good to be out there. 

But then she left. And... well, this all started within just a few weeks of her leaving for basic training. The first week she was gone, the house was just really quiet, and I was mostly just anxious, you know? Constantly checking my phone even though I knew perfectly well they confiscate their phones the second they get off the bus at Fort Sill. But by week two or week three? That's when the bottom just completely fell out. That's when I walked into the garage, looked at my welding gear, and realized I had absolutely zero desire to put my hood on. 

It was like a switch flipped. Before she got on that bus, I had a life, I had things I liked doing to unwind after a long shift at the shop. I looked forward to my weekends. But right around that two or three-week mark after she left, that's when everything just went totally gray. So yeah, it's definitely connected. I was totally fine before, and now I just can't bring myself to care about any of it.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to find enjoyable since your daughter left?

Yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it's completely gone. The interest, the enjoyment, whatever you want to call it. It's just... poof. Gone. Like I told you with the boat and the scrap metal sculptures, I just don't have it in me anymore. 

And it's wild because I used to be someone who couldn't sit still. If I wasn't at the shop, I was tinkering, I was fixing something, I was out on the water. I liked keeping my hands busy, it's just how I'm wired. But now, since she shipped out to Fort Sill, I walk past the garage and I don't even want to open the door. I know my welding hood is sitting right there on the bench exactly where I left it the week before she left, right next to this half-finished little owl I was making out of some leftover aluminum diamond plate. I was actually making it for her, you know? Just a little something to put on her desk or whatever they have in the barracks, but I didn't finish it in time before she had to leave. And now I think about it sitting out there and I just feel sick to my stomach. I don't want to touch it. I don't want to touch any of it. 

So yeah, absolutely, I've lost all interest. I just spend my weekends sitting on the couch with the TV on, usually just some old reruns on cable, not even really watching it. I just leave it on to let the noise fill up the house because it's way too quiet without her here. If it's quiet, I just start thinking too much, and then I'm crying again. So, yes, exactly what I was saying before, the enjoyment is just completely wiped out. I don't care about my hobbies at all right now.
Do you feel like you've lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy since your daughter left for basic training?

Well, yeah, like I... I feel like we're just going in circles here a bit, Doc, because it's exactly what I was just telling you about the garage and the boat. The pleasure, the interest, it's all the same thing to me right now. It's just zero. Nada. 

I mean, take the boat, for instance. I've had that old aluminum bass boat for, gosh, probably twelve years now. Bought it off a guy named Hank who used to work at the shop before he retired and moved down to Florida. It's got this little 15-horsepower outboard motor that always takes exactly three pulls to start—never two, never four, always three. And I used to love that. I loved the ritual of it. I loved hooking the trailer up to my truck on a Saturday morning before the sun even came up, stopping at the gas station on the corner of 4th and Elm to get my coffee and a couple of those terrible powdered donuts, and just getting out on the water. Even if I didn't catch a single fish all day, which, let's be honest, was most days, I just loved the feeling of it. The way the water smelled, the way the wind felt. 

But now? The thought of going through all that trouble, of backing the truck up to the hitch, of driving out to the lake... it just sounds exhausting. It doesn't sound fun. It doesn't sound pleasurable. It just sounds like a whole lot of effort for absolutely no payoff. Because if I'm out there on the lake, sitting in the quiet, I'm just going to be thinking about her. I'm going to be wondering if she's getting yelled at by some drill sergeant, or if she's eating enough, or if she's regretting signing that contract. And that's not pleasurable. That's just torture. So, yeah, the pleasure is gone. Completely gone. Just like I said before.
How long have you felt like you've lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?

Well, again, I feel like I'm repeating myself a little, but... it’s been about a month. It’s been exactly a month and, what, maybe three days since she actually got on that bus. We dropped her off on a Tuesday morning, crack of dawn, pouring rain... I remember the windshield wipers on my truck were squeaking the whole drive there, which usually drives me absolutely crazy and I'd be pulling over to fix it, but I didn't even care that day. 

Anyway, it's been about a month since my daughter left, and I’ve been struggling like this basically since then. Like I told you, maybe that very first week I was mostly just jittery and anxious, pacing holes in the living room rug, but this... this total heavy, empty feeling where I don't want to touch my welding gear or take the boat out? That locked in right after, and it's been my life for the rest of the month. Every single day of it. 

I keep looking at the calendar in the kitchen—it's one of those big ones with the classic cars on it that the auto parts store gives out for free every December—and I just stare at the weeks crossed off since she left, and I realize I haven't done a single thing I used to enjoy in all that time. Just thirty-something days of absolutely nothing but clocking in at the sheet metal shop, coming home, and sitting in the quiet on the couch. It feels like it's been a year, honestly, but yeah on the calendar, it's been about a month of feeling exactly like this.
Do you feel depressed for most of every day?

Well, no, not... not depressed, exactly. I mean, I don't think so. It's more just... empty, you know? Like I'm just going through the motions. I wake up, I make my coffee—usually just instant these days, because who has the energy to actually brew a pot when it's just me?—and I go to the shop. I do my shift, bending the metal, running the brake press, listening to the guys complain about the foreman, and then I come home. 

But depressed? I don't know if I'd use that word. I'm just... I'm just so focused on her, and the fact that she's gone, and how quiet the house is. Like I was saying about the TV, I just leave it on for the noise. It's just a constant, heavy feeling of missing her, and worrying about her, and not wanting to do anything else. But I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking my life is over or anything like that. It's just that my life feels like it's on pause until she gets back, or until I know she's okay. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed most of the day. Just... drained. And sad she's not here. But not depressed.
For how long have you been feeling this emptiness and lack of interest in activities?

Doc, are you... did you not hear me earlier? I feel like we're going in circles again. I swear I just answered this exact same question like two minutes ago. Like I was just saying, it’s been about a month. It’s been a month since my daughter left, and I’ve been struggling like this pretty much ever since then. 

I know I already told you about the big classic car calendar in my kitchen and counting the days, but yeah, that's the timeline. One month. Though, honestly, when you ask me how long it's been, saying "a month" just doesn't really do it justice. Because when you're waking up every single day to a house that's completely silent, and you're drinking that terrible instant coffee, and you're driving to the sheet metal shop just feeling completely hollowed out... a month feels like an absolute eternity. Every eight-hour shift at the brake press feels like a week, and every weekend where I don't take the boat out feels like a month all on its own. 

So on paper, yes, it's been about a month since she got on that bus in the pouring rain, but in my head, I've been stuck in this empty rut for what feels like a lifetime. But yeah, to answer your question again... a month.

My sister, Sarah, she lives about forty minutes away in the next county over, and she usually hosts this big barbecue on the last Sunday of the month. But this last time, a couple of weeks ago, I just... I couldn't do it. She called me on Thursday to see what I was bringing—I usually make this potato salad that everyone loves, the one with the dill and the hard-boiled eggs—and I just told her I wasn't feeling up to it. I think I blamed it on a headache, or maybe I said my shoulder was acting up again from work. I can't even remember the exact excuse.

And it's not just family. The guys at the shop, we usually go grab a beer at O'Malley's after our shift on Fridays. It's kind of a tradition. We wash up, change out of our work boots, and just go complain about the foreman for an hour or two before heading home. I haven't been in... gosh, since before she left. Last Friday, Dave—he's the guy who works the plasma cutter next to my station—he actually came over and tapped me on the shoulder and said, "Hey, you coming with us today? First round's on me." And I just looked at him and said no, I had to get home. 

It's just that, if I go, people are going to ask. They're going to say, "How's she doing?" or "Have you heard from her?" or "Wow, the house must be so quiet!" And they mean well, I know they do. Just sitting there bawling until I have to wipe my face with a fast-food napkin and go inside and pretend I'm fine. 

But I'm not fine. I'm actually messing up at work, which is really bad because I'm usually the one the foreman relies on. I'm missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for literally years—basic TIG welding seams that I could normally do in my sleep, and I'm blowing through the metal or messing up the bead because my brain is just somewhere else. And then I get frustrated, and I end up snapping at the younger guys on the floor. There's this one kid, Tyler, he's just an apprentice, barely older than my daughter, and I completely bit his head off on Tuesday just because he asked to borrow my angle grinder. I felt terrible about it later, but my nerves are just so completely shot. I just don't have the patience or the energy for any of it anymore, let alone hobbies.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive depressed mood
doctor.question: Do you feel depressed most of the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood most of the day, which is a criterion for Major Depressive Disorder. My symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder does not include a specific item for depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I don't... I don't know if I'd use that word. Depressed. Because when I hear that word, I think of, you know, those commercials on TV with the lady staring out a rainy window looking miserable, or... well, like my Aunt Carol. She's my mom's older sister, lives up in Dayton, and she had real, actual depression back in the nineties. Like, she wouldn't get out of bed for weeks at a time. We'd go over there to check on her, and the house would be pitch black, all the curtains pulled tight, smelling like stale cigarettes and unwashed laundry, and she wouldn't even get up to feed her own cats. That's what being depressed most of the day looks like to me. 

But me? I get out of bed. I make my coffee—just Folgers, nothing fancy, I use the same old drip machine I've had for ten years—and I pack my lunch, usually just some turkey on wheat and a bag of pretzels, and I lace up my steel-toed boots. I drive to the shop every single day. I'm functioning, mostly. I mean, yeah, I just told you about how I break down in the truck before my shift, and how my nerves are shot and I'm messing up my welds and snapping at poor Tyler, but once I'm actually on the floor? When I've got my welding hood down and the sparks are flying and the shop radio is blasting some classic rock station over the noise of the grinders? I'm not sitting there feeling depressed. 

I'm just... running on empty. Autopilot. It’s exactly like I was saying before about not feeling sad most of the day. It's not this deep, dark depression from morning till night. It's just a big, blank space where my normal life used to be before she got on that Greyhound. The breakdowns in the truck, that's just... that's just the pressure boiling over, I guess. But the rest of the day, the bulk of the day? I'm just going through the motions. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed most of the day. I'm just trying to survive until it's time to clock out.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminished interest in activities
doctor.question: Do you find that you have less interest in the things you used to enjoy compared to before your daughter left?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I was managing okay before my daughter shipped out, and this all started within a few weeks of her leaving for basic training.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to compare the patient's current symptoms (loss of interest) to the period before the stressor (daughter leaving), which addresses the timeline of symptom onset relative to the stressor.

patient.answer:
Oh, completely. It's... it's like a night and day difference, honestly. Because I was managing just fine before my daughter shipped out. I really was. I mean, we were so busy those last couple of months, running around town getting those specific thick green socks the recruiter told her to buy, making sure all her paperwork was in order, having family over for a going-away dinner... I was stressed, sure, but a normal kind of stressed. I was still doing my metal sculptures in the garage after work, still taking the boat out. 

I actually remember the Sunday right before she left. I was out on the water by 6 AM, drinking my coffee out of this old dented Stanley thermos I take everywhere, just watching the mist burn off the lake. I felt completely normal. I enjoyed it. It felt good to be out there. 

But then she left. And... well, this all started within just a few weeks of her leaving for basic training. The first week she was gone, the house was just really quiet, and I was mostly just anxious, you know? Constantly checking my phone even though I knew perfectly well they confiscate their phones the second they get off the bus at Fort Sill. But by week two or week three? That's when the bottom just completely fell out. That's when I walked into the garage, looked at my welding gear, and realized I had absolutely zero desire to put my hood on. 

It was like a switch flipped. Before she got on that bus, I had a life, I had things I liked doing to unwind after a long shift at the shop. I looked forward to my weekends. But right around that two or three-week mark after she left, that's when everything just went totally gray. So yeah, it's definitely connected. I was totally fine before, and now I just can't bring myself to care about any of it.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminished interest in activities
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to find enjoyable since your daughter left?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest in enjoyable activities), which is a symptom of major depressive disorder and not a distinct criteria key in my Adjustment Disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it's completely gone. The interest, the enjoyment, whatever you want to call it. It's just... poof. Gone. Like I told you with the boat and the scrap metal sculptures, I just don't have it in me anymore. 

And it's wild because I used to be someone who couldn't sit still. If I wasn't at the shop, I was tinkering, I was fixing something, I was out on the water. I liked keeping my hands busy, it's just how I'm wired. But now, since she shipped out to Fort Sill, I walk past the garage and I don't even want to open the door. I know my welding hood is sitting right there on the bench exactly where I left it the week before she left, right next to this half-finished little owl I was making out of some leftover aluminum diamond plate. I was actually making it for her, you know? Just a little something to put on her desk or whatever they have in the barracks, but I didn't finish it in time before she had to leave. And now I think about it sitting out there and I just feel sick to my stomach. I don't want to touch it. I don't want to touch any of it. 

So yeah, absolutely, I've lost all interest. I just spend my weekends sitting on the couch with the TV on, usually just some old reruns on cable, not even really watching it. I just leave it on to let the noise fill up the house because it's way too quiet without her here. If it's quiet, I just start thinking too much, and then I'm crying again. So, yes, exactly what I was saying before, the enjoyment is just completely wiped out. I don't care about my hobbies at all right now.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminished interest or pleasure in most activities
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've lost pleasure in the things you used to enjoy since your daughter left for basic training?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking about the loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia) in activities since the daughter left. This symptom is not present in the patient's symptom profile (the profile includes Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response, additional requirements 1 and 2, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, like I... I feel like we're just going in circles here a bit, Doc, because it's exactly what I was just telling you about the garage and the boat. The pleasure, the interest, it's all the same thing to me right now. It's just zero. Nada. 

I mean, take the boat, for instance. I've had that old aluminum bass boat for, gosh, probably twelve years now. Bought it off a guy named Hank who used to work at the shop before he retired and moved down to Florida. It's got this little 15-horsepower outboard motor that always takes exactly three pulls to start—never two, never four, always three. And I used to love that. I loved the ritual of it. I loved hooking the trailer up to my truck on a Saturday morning before the sun even came up, stopping at the gas station on the corner of 4th and Elm to get my coffee and a couple of those terrible powdered donuts, and just getting out on the water. Even if I didn't catch a single fish all day, which, let's be honest, was most days, I just loved the feeling of it. The way the water smelled, the way the wind felt. 

But now? The thought of going through all that trouble, of backing the truck up to the hitch, of driving out to the lake... it just sounds exhausting. It doesn't sound fun. It doesn't sound pleasurable. It just sounds like a whole lot of effort for absolutely no payoff. Because if I'm out there on the lake, sitting in the quiet, I'm just going to be thinking about her. I'm going to be wondering if she's getting yelled at by some drill sergeant, or if she's eating enough, or if she's regretting signing that contract. And that's not pleasurable. That's just torture. So, yeah, the pleasure is gone. Completely gone. Just like I said before.

target_item.name: Duration

patient.answer:
Well, again, I feel like I'm repeating myself a little, but... it’s been about a month. It’s been exactly a month and, what, maybe three days since she actually got on that bus. We dropped her off on a Tuesday morning, crack of dawn, pouring rain... I remember the windshield wipers on my truck were squeaking the whole drive there, which usually drives me absolutely crazy and I'd be pulling over to fix it, but I didn't even care that day. 

Anyway, it's been about a month since my daughter left, and I’ve been struggling like this basically since then. Like I told you, maybe that very first week I was mostly just jittery and anxious, pacing holes in the living room rug, but this... this total heavy, empty feeling where I don't want to touch my welding gear or take the boat out? That locked in right after, and it's been my life for the rest of the month. Every single day of it. 

I keep looking at the calendar in the kitchen—it's one of those big ones with the classic cars on it that the auto parts store gives out for free every December—and I just stare at the weeks crossed off since she left, and I realize I haven't done a single thing I used to enjoy in all that time. Just thirty-something days of absolutely nothing but clocking in at the sheet metal shop, coming home, and sitting in the quiet on the couch. It feels like it's been a year, honestly, but yeah on the calendar, it's been about a month of feeling exactly like this.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not... not depressed, exactly. I mean, I don't think so. It's more just... empty, you know? Like I'm just going through the motions. I wake up, I make my coffee—usually just instant these days, because who has the energy to actually brew a pot when it's just me?—and I go to the shop. I do my shift, bending the metal, running the brake press, listening to the guys complain about the foreman, and then I come home. 

But depressed? I don't know if I'd use that word. I'm just... I'm just so focused on her, and the fact that she's gone, and how quiet the house is. Like I was saying about the TV, I just leave it on for the noise. It's just a constant, heavy feeling of missing her, and worrying about her, and not wanting to do anything else. But I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking my life is over or anything like that. It's just that my life feels like it's on pause until she gets back, or until I know she's okay. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel depressed most of the day. Just... drained. And sad she's not here. But not depressed.

patient.answer:
Doc, are you... did you not hear me earlier? I feel like we're going in circles again. I swear I just answered this exact same question like two minutes ago. Like I was just saying, it’s been about a month. It’s been a month since my daughter left, and I’ve been struggling like this pretty much ever since then. 

I know I already told you about the big classic car calendar in my kitchen and counting the days, but yeah, that's the timeline. One month. Though, honestly, when you ask me how long it's been, saying "a month" just doesn't really do it justice. Because when you're waking up every single day to a house that's completely silent, and you're drinking that terrible instant coffee, and you're driving to the sheet metal shop just feeling completely hollowed out... a month feels like an absolute eternity. Every eight-hour shift at the brake press feels like a week, and every weekend where I don't take the boat out feels like a month all on its own. 

So on paper, yes, it's been about a month since she got on that bus in the pouring rain, but in my head, I've been stuck in this empty rut for what feels like a lifetime. But yeah, to answer your question again... a month.
